description: Evaluation benchmark for the mock evaluator. Each case is a (question context, answer) pair with an expected category. Run with: python scripts/run_benchmark.py

categories.concise_correct: short but correct answers -> full credit
categories.alternative_valid: differently worded but correct answers -> full credit
categories.partial: answers covering part of the rubric -> partial, 2 <= score < 7
categories.incorrect: answers stating a known misconception -> capped at 4.5
categories.irrelevant: off-topic answers (even if technical) -> capped at 2.5
categories.keyword_stuffing: dense vocabulary with no structure -> nonsense, capped at 1.5
categories.unknown: honest 'I don't know' -> knowledge_gap, capped at 2
categories.scenario: good answer to a scenario question
categories.debugging: good answer to a debugging question
categories.coding: good answer to a coding question
categories.system_design: good answer to a system design question

cases.answer: Python is dynamically typed, so a variable can rebind to different types at runtime. Values are mutable or immutable depending on their type, and the common built-ins are int, float, str, list, dict, tuple and set.

Decorators are functions that take a callable and return a wrapped callable. They modify or extend behaviour without changing the original source. Common uses are logging, timing, caching and auth, and functools.wraps preserves metadata.

Indexes speed up lookups by scanning less data. A B-tree structure lets the database locate rows quickly, at the cost of write overhead and storage. Partial and covering indexes can shrink that trade-off.
FastAPI dependencies use Depends() to share reusable logic. A dependency can be request-scoped, like a database session or the current user. Tests override dependencies to inject fakes.
An image is a read-only template, while a container is a running instance of that image. Dockerfiles describe layers, and because images are cached, builds reuse unchanged layers.

I would use a set to deduplicate the names, because set membership and insertion are average O(1), which beats scanning a list or tuple. If I needed to store counts per name I'd use a dict with the same time complexity. Choosing the right structure for the problem is the key trade-off.

Transactions give ACID properties: a transaction begins, commits or rollback as one unit. MVCC gives isolation levels so concurrent readers see consistent snapshots. Locks and deadlocks still need care.
I'd check whether the endpoint is declared def or async def. A blocking call inside async code stalls the event loop, so sync I/O belongs in the threadpool; awaiting keeps the loop from blocking.
Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE and read the plan output. If I see a seq scan where an index scan should be, I check for missing statistics or outdated plans, and I look for N+1 queries.
Use a multi-stage build: a builder stage compiles, then a slim runtime stage copies the artifact, keeping image size small. Order instructions so hot layers stay cached and rebuilds are fast.

Define a function with default arguments. Defaults are evaluated once at definition time, so use None for mutable defaults. When calling it, *args and **kwargs accept flexible arguments. Scope follows the LEGB rule: local, enclosing, global, builtins.

cases.answer: A load balancer distributes traffic across servers and performs health checks so requests only go to healthy instances. L4 balancing routes on IP and port, while L7 can route on HTTP paths; the trade-off is that L7 is more flexible but adds latency.
Use cache-aside or write-through, set a TTL, and plan invalidation so stale data is bounded. The main risk is a cache stampede when many clients miss at once.
